catalog_quote: If the pitch on individual syllables brings about different meanings in words which are otherwise segmentally identical in a language, then that language is a tone language (Bodomo, 1997:13). There are two types of tones: register (level), and contour tones. Sɛkpɛlé has two register tones: high and low. Tones are used to contrast mono-syllabic words such as the following: 5) tó ‘throw’ tò ‘build’ 6) té ‘sell’ tè ‘know’ 7) ká ‘drive’ kà ‘insult’ ... Contour tones occur in cases where there are identical adjacent vowels differing only in tone, resulting in automatic lengthening for either a rising or falling tone ... There are two functions of tone: lexical and grammatical. The lexical function of tone applies to examples 5 to 8. new_statements.rule_in_words: Sɛkpɛlé is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone on every syllable; contour tones arise from sequences of identical vowels with different tones. The source says nothing about word stress at all — no prominence rule, no claim that stress is absent — so there is no stress placement to record. (Ameka 2009 JWAL p. 141 instead reports three level tones H, M, L plus falling and rising, likewise without any stress statement.)
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only prosodic variation noted is dialectal: 'there seems to be some variation in terms of accent and style. Situnkpa seems to have some variant intonation' (p. 37, §1.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described on syllables and words (lexical contrast in monosyllables, grammatical contrast on subject-cross-reference prefixes); intonation is treated as sentence-level (rising H over the final word for questions).
new_statements.identity_note: Delalorm 2016 describes Sɛkpɛlé proper (the Situnkpa/Semate/Sela varieties of the Likpe traditional area), explicitly setting aside Sekwá (Bakwa, Todome) and Sɛlɛ/Santrokofi (Glottolog sele1249) as other members of the Sele continuum. Funke 1911, listed by Glottolog under sekp1241, is a description of Santrokofi (sele1249), not Sɛkpɛlé.

new_statements.quote: Die Tonbezeichnungen sind ebenfalls ganz unverändert gelassen. Man wird annehmen dürfen, daß es sich im wesentlichen um Tonhöhen handelt; der Akut bedeutet hohen, der Gravis tiefen Ton. Funke bezeichnet außerdem Mitteltöne, fallende und steigende Töne.
new_statements.translation: The tone markings have likewise been left entirely unchanged. One may assume that they essentially represent pitch levels; the acute denotes a high tone, the grave a low tone. Funke additionally marks mid tones, falling and rising tones.

Surrounding secti…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Delalorm 2016 statement (Sɛkpɛlé is a tone language; no stress statement) and with Ameka 2009; it adds nothing about stress. Westermann's tone note is a remark on Funke's transcription of all his languages (Likpe, Bowili, Akpafu), not a Likpe-specific analysis; his H/L (+ Funke's mid, falling, rising) is consistent with Delalorm's two register tones H/L plus contour tones from vowel sequences and with Ameka's three-level H/M/L description. The catalog record's rule field is empty, so nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement on word stress at all. The article is a grammar sketch (gender, case, noun classes, pronouns, numerals, verb) plus wordlists compiled from Missionary E. Funke's field notes, with no Lautlehre/phonology section; a search of the whole article for betont/Betonung/Akzent/Nachdruck finds nothing (the only 'betont' hits are in the East-Asian part of the volume). The one prosodic statement is the editor's note that the tone marks in Funke's material (Likpe, Bowili, Akpafu) are pitch marks: acute = high, grave = low, plus mid, falling and rising tones. Inside the Likpe section tone is invoked three times in passing: the stem syllable -na of ethnonyms is 'tieftonig' (low-toned) (p. 7), the demonstrative namfo 'this/that' is distinguished 'mit verschiedenem Tonfall' (p. 9), and the ordinals show 'Tonverschiebungen' (tone shifts) (p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Likpe' is the Ewe exonym for Sɛkpɛlé (Glottolog sekp1241); the Likpe data come exclusively from Missionary Emil Funke's notes (article preface, p. 1). The same article also treats Bowili (= Tuwuli), Akpafu (= Siwu), Adele and the extinct Boro, which are separate GTM languages; the tone-mark note on p. 2 covers Funke's transcription of Likpe, Bowili and Akpafu jointly, and Mischlich's Adele/Boro material separately.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Sɛkpɛlé phonology' (pp. 60-73); §3.2 'Tone and intonation' pp. 66-68 (PDF pp. 67-69): two register tones H and L with lexical and grammatical (TAM) function; falling/rising contours arise from adjacent identical vowels differing in tone; intonation (rising for questions) marked as H across the final word. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the thesis (only 'distress'); no statement on word-level prominence. Live CORE URL 404s and eprints.soas.ac.uk does not resolve; downloaded from the the Internet Archive copy of CORE (2019-04-15).
